name: Keto diet

image.caption: LOW CARB KETO FRIED CHICKEN by Keto Diet Delish Medium

lead: The keto diet limits carbohydrate so heavily that the body produces ketones from fat. People use it to lose body fat quickly and look leaner in the face and physique, and some also pursue it for skin and hormone benefits. Communities share before-and-after photos and weight-loss reports.

With carbs restricted, the liver makes ketone bodies that substitute for glucose, and appetite often drops while water is shed. Reviews find short-term loss greater than low-fat diets, with the gap shrinking over time; higher-quality meta-analyses find little difference over longer periods, and researchers attribute most loss to calorie intake and adherence.

paras: Followers build meals around meat, fish, eggs, oils and low-carb vegetables, keeping carbs very low and protein adequate. Many see an early scale drop in the first week or two, partly water, with fat loss following over weeks.

Reported effects include constipation, headache, cramps and raised LDL cholesterol; in children on the medical diet, kidney stones and slowed growth occur. Rare ketoacidosis cases exist. The American Heart Association says evidence is insufficient to support it for heart health.

chain: Appetite drops and water is shed
angle.text: Very low carbs and high fat reduce appetite and shed water, helping people lose body fat and look leaner. Trials show short-term weight loss with little difference from other diets once calories are matched.

lead: The ketogenic (keto) diet is a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat, adequate-protein eating pattern that shifts the body toward burning fat and producing ketone bodies. It originated as a medical therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy, mainly in children, and has since become a mainstream weight-loss diet. [1][2]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to lose body fat quickly and look leaner for facial and physique appearance, and members post before-and-after photos and weight-loss reports. [3][4]

Reviews describe the weight-loss evidence as mixed: low-carbohydrate diets can produce more loss than low-fat diets in the short term, but higher-quality meta-analyses find little or no difference over longer periods, and researchers attribute most loss to calorie restriction and adherence. Professional bodies such as the American Heart Association have said evidence is insufficient to support the diet for heart health. [2][5]
infobox: Often under about 50 g per day (definitions vary) [2]
Classic 4:1, MCT, modified Atkins, very low-calorie ketogenic [1][2]

paras: The classic medical version uses a 4:1 ratio of fat to combined protein and carbohydrate by weight. The MCT version uses medium-chain triglyceride oil, which permits more carbohydrate and protein. Weight-loss versions are defined in several ways, including under about 50 g of carbohydrate a day, a very low-calorie ketogenic diet capped at 800 kcal per day, and a modified Atkins approach under 10 g of carbohydrate a day. [1][2]
Definitions of low-carbohydrate eating vary between organisations, which complicates comparison of studies. [2]

Physicians in antiquity treated epilepsy with dietary measures, and fasting was studied for seizures in the early twentieth century. The term ketogenic diet is credited to Russell Wilder of the Mayo Clinic, who ran the first epilepsy trial of it in 1921, and Mynie Peterman formalised the classic diet in the 1920s. Use declined after phenytoin was discovered in 1938 and revived after the Charlie Foundation was founded in 1994 and a 1997 television film dramatised the diet. [1]

Low-carbohydrate weight-loss diets have a separate lineage: William Banting's 1863 Letter on Corpulence and Robert Atkins's 1972 Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution, which was widely criticised by mainstream medicine at the time. Low-carbohydrate diets were among the most popular in the United States in the late 1990s and early 2000s. [2] By 2020 the keto diet was reported to be the most Googled diet in the United States, and the global ketogenic diet market was valued at about 9.57 billion US dollars in 2019. [6]

Reviews report that low-carbohydrate diets can produce more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the advantage fading over time. A 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years, and an Endocrine Society statement noted that with calories held constant, body-fat accumulation does not appear to be affected even by pronounced changes in the fat to carbohydrate ratio. A 2017 review concluded that loss is mainly driven by calorie restriction and adherence rather than diet type. [2]

A review of the ketogenic diet and energy expenditure examined whether ketogenic diets change metabolic rate during weight loss. [7] A 2020 review of the diet's pros and cons noted that few randomized trials of diets have addressed weight loss and cardiovascular outcomes together. [5]
In children on the medical diet, reported effects include constipation, raised blood lipids (affecting up to 60 percent), kidney stones in roughly 1 in 20, slowed growth and fractures. [1]

For weight-loss versions, constipation, headache, bad breath, muscle cramps and weakness are commonly reported, and rare cases of ketoacidosis and nutrient-deficiency complications have been described. Long-term use can raise total and LDL cholesterol. A 2024 laboratory study reported that a ketogenic diet promoted tumor metastasis in mouse models through a BACH1-related mechanism; its relevance to humans has not been established. [2][8]

Dietary guidance bodies have not endorsed the pattern for the general public: the American Heart Association (2021) said evidence is insufficient to support popular diets such as ketogenic, and the British Dietetic Association listed it among its worst celebrity diets in 2018. [2]

Members of looksmax.org discuss keto as a fat-loss route and post physique photos asking whether they look leaner on it. [4] Some members dispute its value or safety, and others argue that calorie control and food quality matter more than diet type. [9] Threads also report personal weight loss over short periods and discuss cholesterol and testosterone. [10][11]

Controlled trials of the ketogenic diet exist for epilepsy, where it is recommended as an adjunct for drug-resistant epilepsy in children by clinical guidelines in the UK. [1] For weight loss, meta-analyses of low-carbohydrate versus low-fat diets are summarised above. [2] No studies were found that tested the diet specifically for facial or other appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org keto appears as one of several fat-loss approaches, with members sharing results and arguing over its safety. [4][9]
